# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia, and its incidence and prevalence are rising globally [1]. The principal hazard of AF is thromboembolic stroke, and the left atrial appendage (LAA) is the dominant source of thrombus in this setting. In a classic surgical review, thrombus was localized to the LAA in 43% of patients with rheumatic heart disease and in 91% of patients with nonrheumatic atrial fibrillation [2]. This anatomic insight provided the conceptual foundation for both surgical appendage exclusion and, subsequently, percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) [3]. Oral anticoagulation (OAC) is highly effective but limited by bleeding risk, drug interactions, and poor adherence, leaving many high-risk patients untreated. LAAC offers a localized, mechanical alternative for stroke prevention.

## Pivotal randomized evidence against warfarin

The first randomized trial, PROTECT AF, established proof of concept. This multicenter study randomized 707 patients with nonvalvular AF and at least one risk factor to either the Watchman device or continued warfarin in a 2:1 ratio [4]. After implantation, warfarin was continued for approximately 45 days, followed by clopidogrel for 4.5 months and lifelong aspirin [4]. The composite endpoint of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death met criteria for noninferiority, though an early periprocedural safety hazard—chiefly pericardial effusion—was identified [4,5]. Longer-term follow-up at 2.3 years confirmed and strengthened these findings [6].

The confirmatory PREVAIL trial enrolled higher-risk patients and incorporated new operators to address safety concerns [7]. Early safety events occurred in 2.2% of the Watchman arm, significantly lower than in PROTECT AF [7]. However, the first coprimary efficacy endpoint did not achieve prespecified noninferiority criteria, in part because of an unexpectedly low event rate in the warfarin group [7,8]. A patient-level meta-analysis of both trials demonstrated comparable efficacy with reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and cardiovascular death [9], and 5-year outcomes showed stroke prevention comparable to warfarin, with additional reductions in major bleeding, particularly hemorrhagic stroke [10]. A pooled net-clinical-benefit analysis reinforced the favorable balance of LAAC versus warfarin [11].

## Patients ineligible for anticoagulation

Because many candidates for LAAC have contraindications to OAC, the nonrandomized ASAP study evaluated implantation followed by antiplatelet therapy alone. This multicenter study enrolled 150 patients with nonvalvular AF and a CHADS2 score ≥1 who were ineligible for oral anticoagulation [12], reporting low ischemic stroke rates and supporting feasibility without a warfarin transition [13]. The EWOLUTION registry extended these observations to a large real-world cohort treated predominantly without OAC [14].

## Device evolution and comparative trials

The next-generation Watchman FLX was evaluated in PINNACLE FLX. In this trial, the device demonstrated 100% effective closure of the LAA and low rates of safety events at 2 years [15]. The Amulet IDE trial provided the first large head-to-head comparison of two devices: the Amulet occluder was noninferior for safety and effectiveness of stroke prevention compared with the Watchman device and superior for LAA occlusion, although procedure-related complications were higher with the Amulet occluder and decreased with operator experience [16]. The SWISS-APERO trial further compared these devices [17], and 5-year Amulet IDE data confirmed durable outcomes for both platforms [18].

## Comparison with direct oral anticoagulants

As DOACs have largely replaced warfarin, the relevant comparison shifted. PRAGUE-17 was a multicenter, randomized, noninferiority trial comparing LAAC with DOACs in high-risk patients [19]. It demonstrated that LAAC was noninferior to nonwarfarin DOACs for preventing major neurological, cardiovascular, or bleeding events, a finding sustained at 4-year follow-up [20]. More recently, the OPTION trial addressed patients undergoing AF ablation: left atrial appendage closure was associated with a lower risk of nonprocedure-related major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding than oral anticoagulation and was noninferior with respect to a composite of death, stroke, or systemic embolism at 36 months [21].

## Procedural complications

Two device-specific complications warrant surveillance. Device-related thrombus (DRT) is uncommon but consequential: in a pooled analysis, DRT was seen in 3.74% of patients, and the rates of stroke and systemic embolism were substantially higher in patients with DRT [22]. Predictors included prior transient ischemic attack or stroke, permanent AF, vascular disease, larger LAA diameter, and lower left ventricular ejection fraction [22]. Registry data further characterize DRT evolution, treatment, and recurrence [23,24]. Peridevice leak is also common; in a registry of 51,333 patients, 73.4% had no leak, 25.8% had small leaks, and 0.7% had large leaks [25], with small leaks associated with a modestly higher thromboembolic risk [26]. Incomplete closure was likewise studied in PROTECT AF substudies [27], and real-world NCDR data confirm high implant success and low complication rates in contemporary practice [28].

## Guidelines and future directions

Reflecting accumulating evidence, the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline upgraded LAAC recommendations [1]: in patients with CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 and a contraindication to long-term OAC, percutaneous LAAO is reasonable (Class 2a), and may be considered in those with high bleeding risk [29]. The SCAI/HRS consensus statement details patient selection, imaging, and procedural standards [30]. Ongoing questions include the optimal antithrombotic regimen, management of leaks and DRT, and the role of LAAC as first-line therapy versus DOACs in broader populations.
